text: An MCP server exposes functionality through three primitives, and the most useful thing to remember about them is who decides when each one gets used -- the model, the application, or the person.

Tools are functions the model actively calls mid-conversation -- search flights, send a message, create a calendar event. Resources are passive, read-only data the application chooses to hand the model as context, the same role a retrieved document plays in RAG. Prompts are pre-built templates a person explicitly invokes.

Here's a real tool definition from MCP's own format: a name, a description, and an inputSchema with typed properties and a required list. Compare it to Lesson 6's get_stock_price schema -- same shape, because it's solving the same problem, now discoverable over the protocol through tools/list and callable through tools/call.

Resources work two ways: a direct resource has a fixed URI pointing at specific data, like a year's calendar. A resource template uses a parameterized URI, like travel activities by city and category, so one template covers a whole family of queries. resources/list, resources/templates/list, and resources/read are the operations behind them.

Keeping tools, resources, and prompts as separate primitives, instead of one generic mechanism, matters later: a host can auto-approve read-only resource access while still requiring approval before a tool call that writes data, because the protocol already tells you which category an action falls into. Next: actually building one of these servers.
